THOUGHT: The child has mucocutaneous bleeding (epistaxis, gum bleeding, petechiae) which points to a platelet-type bleeding diathesis rather than a coagulation factor defect (coagulation profile is normal). Platelet count (280,000/μL) and smear morphology are normal, so thrombocytopenia and platelet production defects are unlikely. The key abnormality is a deficiency of GPIIb/IIIa (αIIbβ3) receptors on platelet surfaces on the ELISA-binding assay. Loss of GPIIb/IIIa impairs platelet aggregation (failure to form fibrinogen bridges), classically causing early-onset mucocutaneous bleeding with normal platelet number and normal PT/aPTT. This pattern fits Glanzmann thrombasthenia and distinguishes it from Bernard–Soulier (GPIb deficiency, associated with giant platelets) and von Willebrand disease (abnormal vWF studies and different platelet aggregation pattern). Thus the most likely diagnosis is Glanzmann thrombasthenia.

DIAGNOSIS: Glanzmann thrombasthenia
